messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nabil is a 40-year-old Arab American paramedic who came to treatment after months of trying to force his life into its old shape and finding that, in crucial ways, he no longer trusted himself inside it. He is married and had spent most of his adult life believing that when something terrible happened, he would know what to do. The event he returns to began on an ordinary evening when his wife was injured and he was with her in the immediate aftermath, close enough to see the damage to her body and to smell the sharp antiseptic of the hospital where she was taken. What remains most vivid for him is not a tidy story but a set of overwhelming sensory fragments: the sight of visible wounds, the look of her as a victim rather than as his wife, the hospital smell that seemed to coat the back of his throat. When the memory comes, it does not feel like remembering. It feels, to him, as if the whole scene is happening again all at once. He can smell it, see it, and feel the same surge of terror in his body. At the same time, there are stretches of the event he cannot account for. He has tried, repeatedly, to piece together what happened minute by minute, but there are parts that simply do not come.

In the first weeks afterward, Nabil told himself he had to keep moving. He tried hard not to think about what had happened, cutting off images as soon as they surfaced and turning his attention to practical tasks. At home he filled his time with projects, errands, and anything that would keep his mind occupied. He also threw himself into work in an almost punishing way, taking on tasks and staying busy because stillness left too much room for the memory to break through. Yet work itself had become one of the places where the trauma felt closest. As a paramedic, he spends his shifts in direct contact with injured people, and visible wounds on patients can stop him internally in an instant. A glimpse of blood or torn skin, the particular antiseptic smell in an emergency department corridor, or even a patient whose face or position reminds him of his wife as he first saw her can pull him into a moment where the past feels fully present. He has found himself standing beside a stretcher while his body reacts as if he is back there, terrified again.

Over time, his relationship to work became conflicted and erratic. Some days he avoided going in altogether, dreading the certainty that he would encounter injury, victims, and hospital smells. On other days he forced himself through shifts and then volunteered for extra responsibilities or buried himself in other tasks afterward, as if nonstop activity could protect him from his own mind. The strain showed. He had increasing difficulty concentrating, which frightened him as much as anything else. He had always depended on his focus in emergencies, and now he noticed himself losing track of details or needing to pull his attention back to the present. He had come to believe that he could no longer rely on himself in the way his job required.

That loss of trust spread into ordinary moments. He startles sharply when touched unexpectedly, even by his wife, with an alarm that feels immediate and out of proportion before he can remind himself where he is. In restaurants, waiting rooms, and even family gatherings, he scans for the seat that feels most protected, preferring a position where no one can come up behind him and where he can see the room. He does not describe this as a habit so much as a necessity; sitting elsewhere leaves him tense and watchful. His wife has noticed how quickly he stiffens in public and how often his attention drifts when she is speaking. Their life has narrowed around his efforts to manage each day without being overtaken.

What weighs heaviest on Nabil is what the event has come to mean about him. He says, with quiet certainty, that he failed to protect the person he loved most. He circles this conviction repeatedly, as if there were some overlooked action that would have changed the outcome. Alongside it is a more global fear that he has been permanently changed for the worse. He does not talk about himself as injured exactly, but as altered in some essential way—less steady, less dependable, no longer the man who could be counted on. Seeking help came after he recognized that both avoiding shifts and forcing himself through them were leaving him more ashamed and more frightened of the next trigger. He is coming now because he wants some way to be with his wife, to do his job, and to encounter the sights and smells of his working life without feeling seized by the same terror. What he fears most is that this is simply who he is now, and what he hopes, cautiously, is that he may not be beyond repair.
